title: SYSK Live: How Game Shows Work
summary: Live recording at the Gothic Theater in Denver, Colorado, in which Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant trace the history of American and international game shows. They cover the British show Spelling Bee, radio and early TV quiz shows such as Truth or Consequences and The $64,000 Question, the 1950s quiz show scandals (Twenty One, Charles Van Doren, Herb Stempel) and the resulting rule changes, Mark Goodson's shift to game shows, and 1970s daytime game show boom (The Price Is Right, Bob Barker, Wheel of Fortune, Match Game, The Newlywed Game). They also discuss the economics of prize budgets and product plugs, 1980s and 1990s shows (Remote Control, Double Dare, American Gladiators), 2000s revivals and imported formats, Japanese game shows such as Takeshi's Castle, and the story of Michael Larson beating Press Your Luck.
topics: Who Wants to Be a Millionaire

segments.title: Opening and framing the game show topic
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck welcome the Denver audience, joke about the Fourth of July and fireworks, and introduce the game show topic.

segments.title: Early game shows: Spelling Bee and radio quiz shows
segments.summary: The first TV game show was the British show Spelling Bee, hosted by Freddie Grisewood. Americans then adopted game shows, with radio shows like The Quiz Show and What's My Line, and Truth or Consequences moved from radio to TV, with its buzzer named Beulah and the town of Hot Springs, New Mexico renaming itself after the show.

segments.title: 1950s quiz show scandal
segments.summary: Quiz shows became top-rated in the 1950s. Producers of Twenty One rigged outcomes, coaching Charles Van Doren while Herb Stempel was a planted, unlikable contestant. Stempel and Tony Jackson went to the press, which dismissed them, until a notebook with the answers surfaced. Congress held hearings, the Communications Act was amended to outlaw dishonest quiz shows, and Van Doren was indicted for perjury.

segments.title: Jeopardy origin and Mark Goodson's game shows
segments.summary: Merv Griffin's wife suggested the answers-as-questions format that became Jeopardy. After the scandals, Mark Goodson and Bill Todman turned quiz shows into game shows, removing the need for knowledge, which led to The Price Is Right.

segments.title: Celebrity panel games and Queen for a Day
segments.summary: Discussion of 1970s celebrity panel shows such as Match Game and Hollywood Squares, where celebrities were often drunk, and The Newlywed Game, including the Holga moment. Queen for a Day featured women telling their hardships while an applause meter decided prizes.

segments.title: Why game shows are cheap: prize budgets and product plugs
segments.summary: Game shows were cheap to make compared with variety shows. Prize budgets, insurance, and structured payouts were discussed, with The Power of Ten as an example. Product plugs traded for prizes made 1970s daytime shows nearly self-funding, and the hosts argue The Price Is Right was an hour-long commercial.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Short ad break during the live show.

segments.title: 1970s daytime boom and long-running hosts
segments.summary: The 1970s daytime game show spasm, with NBC running multiple game shows each weekday, led to Wheel of Fortune becoming the longest-running syndicated game show. Discussion covers Pat Sajak and Vanna White, Sajak's late-night show, and Vanna White's record for applause.

segments.title: Bob Barker and 1980s game shows
segments.summary: Bob Barker's hosting career timeline is covered, including Truth or Consequences and The Price Is Right. The 1980s brought revivals of older shows, along with experiments like Just Men!, hosted by Betty White, Win, Lose or Draw, Double Dare, and Remote Control on MTV.

segments.title: Early 1990s decline and 2000s revival
segments.summary: Game shows waned in the late 1980s and early 1990s, with daytime shows like Family Feud and The Price Is Right surviving, and talk shows and softer news replacing them. Game shows returned in the late 1990s and 2000s with imported formats such as Who Wants to Be a Millionaire, The Weakest Link, and Deal or No Deal. Reality competition shows like American Gladiators and American Ninja Warrior are compared.
topics: Who Wants to Be a Millionaire

segments.title: International game shows and Takeshi's Castle
segments.summary: Game shows are produced worldwide, including Let's Make a Deal in France, The Price Is Right in the UK, and a Russian show called Intercept. Japan is noted for extreme game shows such as Takeshi's Castle and Downtown no Gaki no Tsukai, with punishment games.

segments.title: Second ad break
segments.summary: Second ad break during the live show.

segments.title: What it is like to be on a game show
segments.summary: Discussion of auditions for Wheel of Fortune and Jeopardy, the difficulty of Jeopardy, and Ken Jennings. Also covers how audiences and contestants experience The Price Is Right, FCC regulation of game show conduct, and the Charles Ingram Millionaire cheating case in the UK.
topics: Who Wants to Be a Millionaire scandal

segments.title: Michael Larson and Press Your Luck
segments.summary: Michael Larson, an ice cream truck driver, studied Press Your Luck episodes for hours and found repeating patterns. On the show he won a record $110,237 by hitting 31 consecutive spins. He later won a radio contest by memorizing serial numbers of dollar bills, and his cash was stolen; he died in 2009 while evading the FBI and IRS. A planned Bill Murray film was scrapped.

segments.title: Closing
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck thank the Denver audience and sign off.
